directAnswer: Pope Gregory IX was Ugolino of Segni, a kinsman of Innocent III and cardinal protector of the Franciscans, who reigned from 1227 to 1241. A friend of St. Francis and St. Clare, he canonized Francis, Anthony of Padua and Dominic, promulgated the Decretals that governed canon law for centuries, commissioned papal inquisitors, and fought a long struggle with Emperor Frederick II.

sections.h2: Ugolino, Friend of Francis and Clare
paras: Ugolino was born at Anagni into the family of the counts of Segni, the same family as Innocent III, who made him a cardinal in 1198. He became cardinal bishop of Ostia in 1206 and served as legate in Germany and northern Italy.

He knew St. Francis personally, and at Francis's request Honorius III named him protector of the Friars Minor. He also guided St. Clare and the Poor Ladies of San Damiano. He was elected pope on March 19, 1227, the day after Honorius died.

Within two years of Francis's death, Gregory canonized him at Assisi on July 16, 1228, and laid the foundation stone of the basilica built in his honor. He canonized St. Anthony of Padua in 1232, less than a year after Anthony's death, St. Dominic in 1234, and St. Elizabeth of Hungary in 1235.

In 1230 his bull Quo elongati ruled that Francis's Testament was not legally binding on the friars and clarified how the brothers could use goods without owning them, decisions that shaped later Franciscan debates over poverty.

When Frederick II again postponed his crusade in 1227, Gregory excommunicated him. Frederick sailed anyway in 1228 and in 1229 recovered Jerusalem by treaty with the sultan of Egypt. Pope and emperor reconciled at San Germano and Ceprano in 1230, but conflict over Lombardy and the Papal States led Gregory to excommunicate Frederick again in 1239.

In 1241 Frederick's fleet captured many prelates traveling to a council Gregory had summoned. With imperial troops near Rome, Gregory died on August 22, 1241. He also supported crusading campaigns in the Baltic region.

sections.h2: The Decretals, Paris and the Inquisition
paras: Gregory commissioned the Dominican St. Raymond of Peñafort to compile a single, official collection of papal decretals. Promulgated in 1234, the Decretals of Gregory IX, also called the Liber Extra, remained a core part of the Church's law until the Code of Canon Law of 1917. In 1231 his bull Parens scientiarum settled a strike at the University of Paris and confirmed the university's rights.

From the early 1230s Gregory commissioned inquisitors, chiefly Dominican friars, to investigate heresy under direct papal authority, which is regarded as the beginning of the papal inquisition. He also ordered an investigation of the Talmud in 1239, which led to its condemnation and burning in Paris in the 1240s, an episode now remembered as a grave injustice to the Jewish people.

keyFacts: Personal name: Ugolino of Segni, born at Anagni
Cardinal protector of the Franciscans; friend of St. Francis and St. Clare
Canonized St. Francis (1228), St. Anthony of Padua (1232) and St. Dominic (1234)
Promulgated the Decretals of Gregory IX (Liber Extra) in 1234
Excommunicated Frederick II in 1227 and again in 1239

faqs.question: How did Gregory IX know St. Francis?
faqs.answer: As Cardinal Ugolino he was the official protector of the Franciscan order and a personal friend of Francis, whom he canonized in 1228, less than two years after his death.

faqs.question: What were the Decretals of Gregory IX?
faqs.answer: An official collection of papal laws compiled by St. Raymond of Peñafort and promulgated in 1234. It remained central to Catholic canon law until 1917.

faqs.question: Did Gregory IX start the inquisition?
faqs.answer: He began appointing papal inquisitors, mostly Dominicans, in the early 1230s, which historians treat as the start of the papal inquisition, building on earlier bishops' inquiries.
